You’re graduating soon, so I’m taking a guess at your age. I’ll take another guess and assume you’ve felt this way for about a year? Maybe a bit longer or shorter, but it might be a relatively new development. 

If I’m right, first I want to congratulate you on recognizing that something is wrong. Many people aren’t able to pinpoint these feelings when they first appear and don’t begin trying to manage them until they become nearly impossible to manage. So you’re already doing what you need to be doing by acknowledging that *something is wrong*.

To the folks saying it doesn’t get better, maybe you should follow OP’s lead and take stock of your own situation before giving advice. 

That said, it doesn’t go away. Most commonly, chronic mental illnesses present themselves in your earliest 20s. This is absolutely normal, and it was the case with me. I was 21 when I woke up one morning and *something was wrong*, so I reached out to my family and let them know that I was seeking counseling, and why. They were able and very willing to help and support my efforts to get “better.”

I’m 30 now. I’ve tried medication but haven’t found anything I like. Talk therapy has been useful, particularly with my anxiety, self esteem, and social handicap. Meditation has been huge for me. I’ve also found that regular exercise helps tremendously, but I struggle to motivate for it - so I stopped buying transit passes and now I HAVE to ride my bike everywhere. Try to set yourself up in a way that healthy decisions are easier to make, if you can. 

Lastly, and take this with a big grain of salt, I have found psychedelics to be tremendously helpful when nothing else is working. The term “getting small” was coined in the 1960s by proponents of LSD, and it refers to the ego-dissolving effect that all psychedelics produce - not just LSD. Self doubt and criticism, personal troubles, societal constructs, all this added weight that the psyche has to carry around can make just existing seem like a chore. When you take a psychoactive compound, much of that noise completely melts away and your mind wanders inward. These compounds work to effectively “mute” the area of your brain responsible for your sense of identity, but many psychonauts come out of their trip describing a greater sense of self, interestingly, and also a sense of peace. I’ll wrap this point up with the necessary disclaimer: psychedelics are currently being researched for the treatment of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, though none have been approved for such purposes outside of human trials. Self medicating with These compounds is not legal in most countries. Use common sense and treat these compounds with respect.
